name: Subword vocabulary induction
characteristic: criterion by which the next vocabulary item is chosen
positive_test: fits a finite token vocabulary to a corpus before any model is trained
negative_test: a fixed hand-written vocabulary or a whitespace split with no induction step
examples: BPE, WordPiece, Unigram LM
notes: tokenizer choice is reported as a method, not a library setting

name: Byte-pair-encoding merges
positive_test: merges the most frequent adjacent pair, iteratively, to a target vocabulary size
negative_test: likelihood-driven vocabulary pruning
examples: BPE, byte-level BPE, SentencePiece-BPE

name: Likelihood-gain merges
positive_test: merges the pair that most increases corpus likelihood under a unigram model
negative_test: pure frequency counting
examples: WordPiece

name: Vocabulary pruning from a superset
positive_test: starts from a large candidate set and removes items that cost least likelihood
negative_test: bottom-up merging
examples: Unigram LM, SentencePiece-Unigram

name: Tokenizer-free byte or character units
positive_test: uses raw bytes or characters, so no vocabulary is induced from data
negative_test: any corpus-fitted vocabulary
examples: ByT5 scheme, CANINE scheme, character-level LM input
notes: boundary: arguably the absence of an algorithm

name: Input-space data augmentation
characteristic: what is transformed and how the transform is chosen
positive_test: replaces or perturbs a training example with a transformed version, leaving the label rule intact
negative_test: transformations applied at test time only; architectural noise layers
examples: RandAugment, CutMix, SpecAugment

name: Geometric and photometric transforms
positive_test: applies a fixed hand-specified image transform family with sampled parameters
negative_test: transforms whose parameters are themselves learned or searched
examples: random resized crop, horizontal flip, rotation, color jitter
notes: named weakly; include only when the paper names the recipe

name: Occlusion and erasing
positive_test: deletes a contiguous region of the input and does not replace it with other data
negative_test: mixing two examples together
examples: Cutout, Random Erasing, GridMask, token dropout

name: Example mixing
positive_test: builds a training example by combining two or more examples and their labels
negative_test: single-example perturbation
examples: mixup, CutMix, Manifold Mixup, FMix, Mosaic, AugMix
notes: label is mixed too, which also touches the objective

name: Searched augmentation policies
positive_test: selects which augmentations to apply by searching over policies against a validation signal
negative_test: a fixed augmentation list chosen by hand
examples: AutoAugment, Fast AutoAugment, RandAugment, TrivialAugment, PBA
notes: sits on two axes at once by construction

name: Text-space augmentation
positive_test: perturbs tokens or re-generates text while preserving the label
negative_test: prompt engineering at inference
examples: EDA, back-translation, synonym substitution, round-trip translation

name: Adversarial example generation
positive_test: constructs an input perturbation that maximises the model's loss under a norm budget
negative_test: random noise with no maximisation step
examples: FGSM, PGD, C&W, AutoAttack
notes: same procedure serves as attack and as training-data source

name: Class-imbalance resampling
characteristic: whether examples are added, removed or synthesised
positive_test: changes the class frequencies seen by the learner, without changing the loss definition
negative_test: a reweighted loss, which is an objective change
examples: SMOTE, ADASYN, Tomek links, NearMiss, random oversampling

name: Dataset curation and selection
characteristic: what score decides whether an example is kept, ordered or weighted
positive_test: selects, deduplicates, weights or orders the training examples before or during fitting
negative_test: generating new examples; transforming individual examples
examples: SemDeDup, DoReMi, curriculum learning

name: Near-duplicate removal
positive_test: removes examples that are near-identical to another under a similarity threshold
negative_test: removing examples for being low-quality rather than redundant
examples: MinHash/LSH dedup, SemDeDup, exact-substring dedup

name: Quality and contamination filtering
positive_test: drops examples scored below a threshold by a classifier, perplexity model or rule
negative_test: dropping examples to balance classes
examples: quality classifier filtering, perplexity filtering, decontamination

name: Domain mixture weighting
positive_test: chooses sampling proportions across labelled data sources
negative_test: choosing which single corpus to use
examples: DoReMi, DoGE, hand-tuned domain weights

name: Curriculum ordering
positive_test: changes the order or schedule in which examples are presented, not which are present
negative_test: changing the set of examples
examples: curriculum learning, self-paced learning, anti-curriculum, sequence-length warmup

name: Active and coreset selection
positive_test: repeatedly selects which unlabelled points to label or keep, using the current model
negative_test: a one-shot random subsample
examples: uncertainty sampling, BALD, core-set selection, GraNd, EL2N

name: Dataset distillation
positive_test: optimises a small synthetic dataset so that training on it reproduces training on the full set
negative_test: compressing the model rather than the data
examples: dataset distillation, gradient matching, distribution matching

name: Classical feature preprocessing
characteristic: what statistic of the training data the transform is fitted to
positive_test: fits a fixed transform to the training split and applies it to every split
negative_test: a transform with no fitted parameters
examples: z-scoring, ZCA whitening, target encoding

name: Location-scale and whitening transforms
positive_test: removes mean and rescales or decorrelates using first and second moments
negative_test: rank-based transforms
examples: standardisation, min-max scaling, PCA whitening, ZCA whitening

name: Rank and quantile transforms
positive_test: maps values through their empirical rank or quantile
negative_test: moment-based rescaling
examples: quantile normalisation, rank-gauss, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson

name: Discretisation and encoding
positive_test: converts a continuous or categorical column into a new coded representation
negative_test: continuous rescaling
examples: equal-width/equal-frequency binning, MDLP, one-hot, target/mean encoding

name: Missing-data imputation
positive_test: fills missing entries with values estimated from observed data
negative_test: dropping incomplete rows
examples: mean/median imputation, MICE, kNN imputation, matrix-completion imputation

name: Feature selection
positive_test: removes input variables before or during fitting based on a relevance score
negative_test: projecting features into a new space
examples: mutual-information filtering, recursive feature elimination, lasso selection, Boruta

name: Synthetic training-data generation
characteristic: what produces the synthetic example
positive_test: creates new training examples from a model, a simulator or a rule, rather than transforming real ones
negative_test: perturbing an existing real example
examples: Self-Instruct, domain randomisation, Evol-Instruct

name: Model-generated corpora
positive_test: a generative model emits the training examples, optionally filtered
negative_test: a human or simulator emits them
examples: Self-Instruct, Alpaca-style generation, Evol-Instruct, synthetic textbooks
notes: overlaps distillation when the generator is a stronger model

name: Simulation and domain randomisation
positive_test: a simulator with randomised parameters emits examples to cross a reality gap
negative_test: data collected in the target domain
examples: domain randomisation, procedural scene generation, sim-to-real pipelines

name: Counterfactual example construction
positive_test: constructs an example differing in one causal factor while holding others fixed
negative_test: arbitrary perturbation with no factor held fixed
examples: counterfactual data augmentation, CAD, minimal-pair generation

name: Exploration rules
characteristic: what quantity drives the deviation from the greedy action
positive_test: decides which action to take for the purpose of gathering data, separately from the update rule
negative_test: a rule that defines the learning target rather than action selection
examples: epsilon-greedy, UCB1, RND
notes: the single most under-named slot in RL papers

name: Undirected stochastic exploration
positive_test: perturbs the greedy action with noise that does not depend on uncertainty
negative_test: noise scaled by a learned or counted uncertainty
examples: epsilon-greedy, Boltzmann/softmax, OU noise, parameter-space noise, NoisyNets

name: Optimism under uncertainty
positive_test: adds a confidence bonus to value estimates and acts greedily on the inflated value
negative_test: sampling from a posterior instead of inflating
examples: UCB1, UCB-V, LinUCB, optimistic initialisation, RLSVI

name: Posterior sampling
positive_test: samples a hypothesis from a posterior and acts greedily with respect to it
negative_test: adding a deterministic bonus
examples: Thompson sampling, bootstrapped DQN, posterior sampling for RL

name: Intrinsic-motivation bonuses
positive_test: adds a learned novelty or prediction-error term into the reward the agent optimises
negative_test: a bonus used only for action selection and never entering the return
examples: RND, ICM, pseudo-counts, Disagreement, NGU, empowerment
notes: also alters the objective, so it carries two roles

name: Diversity-driven and archive-based search
positive_test: maintains an archive of behaviours and explicitly selects for behavioural novelty
negative_test: selecting for return only
examples: Go-Explore, novelty search, MAP-Elites, DIAYN, DADS

name: Experience storage and relabelling
characteristic: what decides which past transition is reused and with what target
positive_test: stores past interaction and re-serves it to the learner, possibly with a changed target
negative_test: generating fresh interaction
examples: uniform replay, PER, HER

name: Uniform experience replay
positive_test: samples stored transitions uniformly at random
negative_test: sampling with a priority or a changed goal
examples: experience replay, replay ratio schedules

name: Priority-weighted replay
positive_test: samples stored transitions in proportion to a learning-progress score
negative_test: uniform sampling
examples: PER, ERE, LAP, topological replay

name: Goal and reward relabelling
positive_test: rewrites the goal or reward of a stored transition so a failure becomes a success
negative_test: reusing a transition with its original reward
examples: HER, hindsight relabelling, GCSL relabelling

name: Opponent and task generation
characteristic: what determines the opponent or task distribution
positive_test: generates the training distribution by playing against or generating versions of the system itself
negative_test: a fixed opponent or fixed task set
examples: self-play, PSRO, PLR

name: Self-play against current or past selves
positive_test: plays the learner against copies of itself drawn from its own training history
negative_test: playing against a fixed scripted opponent
examples: naive self-play, fictitious self-play, self-play with opponent pools

name: Population and league training
positive_test: maintains a population with explicit exploiter or niche roles and matchmaking
negative_test: a single-copy self-play loop
examples: PSRO, double oracle, AlphaStar league, NFSP

name: Automatic environment curricula
positive_test: generates or selects environments or goals to match the agent's current competence
negative_test: a fixed environment distribution
examples: POET, PLR, ADR, ALP-GMM, asymmetric self-play

name: Dynamic programming for MDPs
positive_test: computes a value or policy by sweeping Bellman backups over a known transition model
negative_test: learning from sampled transitions without a given model
examples: policy iteration, value iteration, generalised policy iteration, asynchronous DP
notes: founder of the whole value-based lineage

name: Temporal-difference learning
positive_test: updates a value estimate toward a bootstrapped target built from the next state's own estimate
negative_test: updating toward a full Monte-Carlo return only
examples: TD(0), TD(lambda), true online TD, GTD

name: Off-policy TD control
positive_test: bootstraps from the max (or an argmax-decoupled estimate) over next-state actions
negative_test: bootstrapping from the action the behaviour policy actually took
examples: Q-learning, Double Q-learning, Expected SARSA(off-policy form)

name: On-policy TD control
positive_test: bootstraps from the action the current policy actually selects
negative_test: bootstrapping from a max over actions
examples: SARSA, Expected SARSA, n-step SARSA

name: Deep Q-networks
positive_test: fits Q-learning with a neural network plus a target network and a replay buffer
negative_test: tabular Q-learning; actor-critic with an explicit policy head
examples: DQN, Double DQN, Dueling DQN, NoisyNet-DQN, Rainbow, Ape-X, R2D2, Munchausen DQN
notes: the canonical "ancestor worth aggregating to"

name: Distributional value learning
positive_test: learns the full return distribution rather than only its expectation
negative_test: learning a scalar expected return
examples: C51, QR-DQN, IQN, FQF

name: Sample-efficient deep value learning
positive_test: raises updates-per-environment-step with explicit remedies for the resulting overfitting
negative_test: scaling data rather than updates
examples: DrQ, SPR, SR-SPR, BBF, REDQ
notes: SPR is multi-parent with self-predictive SSL

name: Policy-gradient methods
positive_test: differentiates expected return with respect to policy parameters via the score-function identity
negative_test: updating a value table or network with no explicit policy parameterisation
examples: REINFORCE, actor-critic, A3C, A2C

name: Actor-critic
positive_test: reduces policy-gradient variance with a learned value baseline or critic
negative_test: using an empirical return baseline only
examples: actor-critic, A3C, A2C, GAE, IMPALA/V-trace, ACER

name: Trust-region and clipped policy updates
positive_test: bounds the size of the policy change per update by a divergence or ratio constraint
negative_test: an unconstrained gradient step on the policy
examples: natural policy gradient, TRPO, PPO, PPO-clip, V-MPO

name: Group-relative policy optimisation
positive_test: replaces the learned critic with a baseline computed across a sampled group of completions
negative_test: using a learned value network as the baseline
examples: GRPO, RLOO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO
notes: the dominant recent RL-for-reasoning branch

name: Deterministic policy gradients
positive_test: backpropagates the critic's gradient through a deterministic actor
negative_test: sampling actions from a stochastic policy and using the score function
examples: DPG, DDPG, TD3, D4PG
notes: requires continuous actions

name: Maximum-entropy RL
positive_test: optimises return plus a policy-entropy term as part of the objective, not as a bonus
negative_test: entropy added only as an auxiliary regulariser with no soft-Bellman consistency
examples: soft Q-learning, SAC, MPO, soft actor-critic variants, REDQ

name: Model-based RL
characteristic: what the learned dynamics model is used for
positive_test: learns a transition or reward model and uses it to improve the policy or the value estimate
negative_test: learning a value or policy directly from environment samples only
examples: Dyna, PETS, Dreamer, MuZero

name: Model-generated experience
positive_test: uses the learned model to synthesise extra transitions for a model-free learner
negative_test: using the model only inside an action-selection search
examples: Dyna, Dyna-Q, MBPO, SLBO

name: Model-predictive control over a learned model
positive_test: re-plans an action sequence at each step by rolling the model forward
negative_test: amortising the plan into a policy network and never re-planning
examples: PILCO, PETS, CEM-MPC, MPPI, iCEM

name: Latent-dynamics world models
positive_test: learns dynamics in a compressed latent space and trains the policy inside it
negative_test: planning directly in observation space
examples: World Models, PlaNet, Dreamer, DreamerV2, DreamerV3, TD-MPC

name: Learned-model tree search
positive_test: combines a learned model with an explicit tree search that produces the acting policy
negative_test: planning by trajectory sampling without a tree
examples: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, EfficientZero, Sampled MuZero
notes: the clearest case of one lineage spanning two roles

name: Offline reinforcement learning
characteristic: how the policy is kept inside the data's support
positive_test: learns a policy from a fixed logged dataset with no further environment interaction
negative_test: collecting new interaction at any point in training
examples: BCQ, CQL, IQL, Decision Transformer

name: Explicit policy constraint
positive_test: penalises or projects the learned policy toward the behaviour policy
negative_test: penalising the value function instead
examples: BCQ, BEAR, TD3+BC, BRAC

name: Pessimistic value penalty
positive_test: lowers values of out-of-distribution actions so they are never selected
negative_test: constraining the policy's action distribution directly
examples: CQL, COMBO, pessimistic MDPs, EDAC

name: Implicit and weighted-regression policy extraction
positive_test: extracts a policy by advantage-weighted regression without querying unseen actions
negative_test: computing a max over actions outside the data
examples: AWR, AWAC, IQL, XQL, SQL

name: Return-conditioned sequence modelling
positive_test: casts control as supervised next-token prediction conditioned on a desired return
negative_test: fitting a value function and improving a policy against it
examples: Decision Transformer, Trajectory Transformer, RvS, Multi-Game DT
notes: signal is a label, not a reward, despite being RL

name: Imitation learning
characteristic: what replaces the reward signal
positive_test: fits a policy from expert demonstrations with no environment reward
negative_test: learning from an environment reward signal
examples: behaviour cloning, DAgger, GAIL

name: Behaviour cloning
positive_test: fits actions to states by supervised regression or classification on demonstrations
negative_test: inferring a reward function first
examples: behaviour cloning, DAgger, DART, ACT, diffusion policy training

name: Inverse reinforcement learning
positive_test: infers a reward function that rationalises the demonstrations, then plans or learns on it
negative_test: directly copying actions
examples: MaxEnt IRL, guided cost learning, AIRL, Bayesian IRL

name: Adversarial imitation
positive_test: trains a discriminator to separate agent from expert transitions and uses it as reward
negative_test: matching actions pointwise
examples: GAIL, DAC, AIRL, f-GAIL

name: Preference-based alignment
characteristic: whether a reward model is fit, and how the policy is updated against preferences
positive_test: optimises a policy against pairwise or ranked human or AI preference judgements
negative_test: optimising against a scalar reward supplied by the environment
examples: RLHF, DPO, GRPO-with-reward-model

name: Reward modelling plus policy optimisation
positive_test: fits an explicit reward model on comparisons, then runs an RL algorithm against it
negative_test: optimising the policy on preferences in closed form, with no reward model
examples: RLHF with PPO, RLAIF, Constitutional AI, reward-model ensembles

name: Direct preference optimisation
positive_test: derives a closed-form policy loss from the preference pairs, skipping the reward model
negative_test: fitting a separate reward network
examples: DPO, IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO, cDPO, CPO

name: Rejection-sampled finetuning
positive_test: samples candidates, keeps the best by a scorer, then does supervised finetuning on them
negative_test: updating with a policy-gradient step
examples: best-of-n finetuning, RAFT, STaR, rejection-sampling SFT, ReST
notes: sits between SFT and RL

name: Verifier-rewarded RL
positive_test: the reward comes from a programmatic checker rather than a learned or human judgement
negative_test: a reward model trained on human comparisons
examples: RLVR, unit-test reward, math-answer-match reward

name: Multi-agent RL
characteristic: how the joint value or joint policy is factored
positive_test: trains two or more interacting policies whose returns depend on each other
negative_test: a single agent in a stationary environment
examples: QMIX, MADDPG, MAPPO

name: Independent learners
positive_test: each agent runs a single-agent algorithm treating others as part of the environment
negative_test: any explicit factorisation of a joint value or a centralised critic
examples: IQL, IPPO, independent A2C

name: Value factorisation
positive_test: decomposes a joint action-value into per-agent terms under a monotonicity or additivity condition
negative_test: learning the joint value without any decomposition
examples: VDN, QMIX, QTRAN, QPLEX, Qatten

name: Centralised critic, decentralised actors
positive_test: trains a critic with access to global state while each actor sees only its own observation
negative_test: both training and execution use only local information
examples: MADDPG, MAPPO, COMA, FACMAC

name: Equilibrium-computing methods
positive_test: computes an approximate equilibrium rather than a best response to fixed others
negative_test: optimising against a frozen opponent
examples: fictitious play, CFR, Deep CFR, NFSP, Nash-Q, regret matching

name: Hierarchical RL
characteristic: what the temporal abstraction is defined over
positive_test: learns a policy over temporally extended sub-policies with their own termination
negative_test: a flat policy over primitive actions
examples: options framework, option-critic, FeUdal networks, HIRO, HAC

name: Bandit algorithms
characteristic: how uncertainty about arm values is turned into a choice
positive_test: selects among actions with immediate feedback and no state transition
negative_test: a setting with state dynamics and delayed credit
examples: UCB1, Thompson sampling, EXP3
notes: shares its characteristic with L.explore by design

name: Stochastic and contextual bandits
positive_test: assumes i.i.d. rewards per arm, possibly conditioned on a context vector
negative_test: an adversarial reward sequence
examples: UCB1, LinUCB, LinTS, Thompson sampling, KL-UCB

name: Adversarial bandits
positive_test: guarantees regret against an arbitrary, possibly adaptive reward sequence
negative_test: an i.i.d. reward assumption
examples: EXP3, EXP4, Tsallis-INF

name: Best-arm identification
positive_test: spends a fixed budget to identify the best arm, not to maximise cumulative reward
negative_test: minimising cumulative regret while acting
examples: successive halving, sequential halving, LUCB, racing

name: Off-policy evaluation and learning
positive_test: estimates the value of a policy from logs collected under a different policy
negative_test: evaluating a policy by running it
examples: inverse propensity scoring, self-normalised IPS, doubly robust OPE, FQE
notes: shares estimators with causal inference

name: Instance-discrimination contrastive learning
positive_test: pulls together views of the same instance and explicitly pushes apart other instances
negative_test: a method with no negative examples in its loss
examples: InstDisc, CPC, MoCo, MoCo v2, MoCo v3, SimCLR, SimCLR v2

name: Cross-modal contrastive alignment
positive_test: contrasts paired items from two different modalities against mismatched pairs
negative_test: contrasting two augmented views of one item
examples: CLIP, ALIGN, SigLIP, AudioCLIP, ImageBind
notes: pairing is a supervision source, which blurs self vs supervised

name: Label-aware contrastive learning
positive_test: treats all same-class examples as positives using ground-truth labels
negative_test: treating only augmented views of one instance as positives
examples: SupCon, contrastive representation distillation

name: Negative-free self-distillation
positive_test: regresses a student view onto a target produced by a momentum or stop-gradient copy
negative_test: a loss containing explicit negative pairs
examples: Mean Teacher, BYOL, SimSiam, DINO, DINOv2
notes: collapse avoidance is the defining engineering problem

name: Redundancy-reduction objectives
positive_test: decorrelates embedding dimensions via a cross-correlation or covariance criterion
negative_test: contrasting whole embeddings against other samples
examples: Barlow Twins, VICReg, VICRegL, W-MSE

name: Clustering-based self-supervision
positive_test: alternates assigning pseudo-cluster labels and predicting them from another view
negative_test: a loss defined directly between embeddings with no assignment step
examples: DeepCluster, SeLa, SwAV, PCL, ODC

name: Masked-input prediction
characteristic: what is masked and what the reconstruction target is
positive_test: hides part of the input and trains the model to recover it from the remainder
negative_test: predicting the next element with no masking of a visible context
examples: BERT MLM, MAE, wav2vec 2.0

name: Masked language modelling
positive_test: masks tokens and predicts their identity from bidirectional context
negative_test: predicting only the next token left to right
examples: CBOW, BERT MLM, RoBERTa, SpanBERT, T5 span corruption, ELECTRA
notes: ELECTRA replaces the target with a detection task

name: Masked visual modelling
positive_test: masks image or video patches and reconstructs pixels, tokens or features
negative_test: reconstructing the whole unmasked image
examples: Context Encoders, BEiT, MAE, SimMIM, iBOT, VideoMAE

name: Masked and contrastive speech modelling
positive_test: masks spans of audio and predicts quantised or clustered units
negative_test: predicting transcribed text
examples: wav2vec, wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM, data2vec

name: Handcrafted pretext tasks
positive_test: invents a label from a known transformation of the input and predicts it
negative_test: predicting part of the raw input content itself
examples: relative patch position, jigsaw, rotation prediction, colourisation, shuffle-and-learn
notes: largely historical; kept as an aggregation ancestor

name: Latent predictive self-supervision
positive_test: predicts the representation of unobserved content rather than its raw content
negative_test: regressing raw pixels or tokens
examples: CPC, I-JEPA, V-JEPA, SPR, PBL
notes: SPR applies this inside RL, hence multi-parent

name: Shallow embedding induction
characteristic: what co-occurrence structure the embedding factorises
positive_test: fits a lookup-table embedding directly from co-occurrence statistics, with no deep encoder
negative_test: training a deep encoder end to end
examples: word2vec, GloVe, fastText, DeepWalk, node2vec, item2vec
notes: produces a model, but the procedure is the entry

name: Autoregressive density modelling
positive_test: factorises the joint density into a product of conditionals and fits each by maximum likelihood
negative_test: fitting a bound on the likelihood or an implicit density
examples: n-gram MLE, neural LM, PixelRNN, PixelCNN, causal LM pretraining, WaveNet training
notes: the dominant pretraining objective; needs its own ancestor

name: Exposure-bias corrections
positive_test: changes which context the model conditions on during training to match inference
negative_test: plain teacher forcing
examples: scheduled sampling, professor forcing, SeqGAN-style corrections

name: Variational autoencoding
positive_test: maximises an evidence lower bound with an amortised inference network
negative_test: maximising exact likelihood; using a discriminator
examples: wake-sleep, VAE, beta-VAE, IWAE, NVAE

name: Discrete-latent autoencoding
positive_test: quantises the latent to a learned codebook and trains through a straight-through estimator
negative_test: a continuous Gaussian latent
examples: VQ-VAE, VQ-VAE-2, VQGAN, FSQ, RQ-VAE
notes: the tokeniser for most latent generative stacks

name: Adversarial generative training
characteristic: which part of the minimax setup is altered
positive_test: trains a generator against a discriminator whose loss it maximises
negative_test: any objective with an explicit likelihood or reconstruction term
examples: GAN, WGAN, StyleGAN, CycleGAN

name: Adversarial divergence variants
positive_test: changes the divergence or the discriminator's loss form
negative_test: changes conditioning or architecture only
examples: LSGAN, WGAN, WGAN-GP, SN-GAN, hinge GAN, f-GAN, relativistic GAN

name: Conditional and translation GANs
positive_test: conditions the generator on a label, image or text and pairs or cycles the mapping
negative_test: unconditional sampling
examples: cGAN, pix2pix, CycleGAN, StarGAN, SPADE

name: Adversarial training stabilisers
positive_test: adds a regulariser or update-timing rule aimed at the minimax dynamics
negative_test: a change in the generator's data distribution
examples: R1 regularisation, instance noise, TTUR, PPL regularisation, ADA

name: Normalizing flows
characteristic: how the invertible map is constructed
positive_test: models density through an exactly invertible map with a tractable Jacobian determinant
negative_test: a non-invertible decoder with a bound
examples: NICE, RealNVP, Glow, MAF, IAF

name: Continuous-time flows
positive_test: defines the map as the solution of a learned ODE rather than a stack of coupling layers
negative_test: discrete stacked bijectors
examples: Neural ODE, FFJORD, rectified flow, flow matching, stochastic interpolants
notes: flow matching is also the modern diffusion-training formulation

name: Score-based and diffusion modelling
positive_test: learns the score or the noise of a progressively corrupted data distribution
negative_test: learning an exact or bounded likelihood of the clean data directly
examples: score matching, denoising score matching, NCSN, DDPM, improved DDPM, EDM, SDE diffusion

name: Guidance of the diffusion trajectory
positive_test: steers sampling with an external or implicit conditional signal during generation
negative_test: conditioning only through the training objective
examples: classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance, ControlNet conditioning, CFG rescaling
notes: role is decoding although the lineage is generative

name: Latent-space diffusion
positive_test: runs the diffusion process in a learned compressed space rather than pixel space
negative_test: diffusing directly on raw observations
examples: latent diffusion, Stable Diffusion training, DiT training

name: Diffusion samplers and distillation
positive_test: reduces the number of denoising steps needed to produce a sample
negative_test: the training procedure that fits the denoiser
examples: DDIM, DPM-Solver, UniPC, progressive distillation, consistency models, LCM
notes: lineage drifts from objective to decoder; see Tensions

name: Energy-based modelling
positive_test: fits an unnormalised energy whose normaliser is never computed exactly
negative_test: a model with a tractable normalising constant
examples: Boltzmann machine, RBM, contrastive divergence, deep belief net, JEM, Langevin EBM

name: Stochastic first-order descent
positive_test: steps the parameters along a stochastic gradient with a scalar step size
negative_test: a per-coordinate or matrix-preconditioned step
examples: Robbins-Monro, SGD, heavy-ball momentum, Nesterov acceleration, averaged SGD

name: Sign-based and normalised updates
positive_test: uses only the sign or the normalised direction of the gradient
negative_test: a magnitude-proportional step
examples: signSGD, Lion, normalised SGD, LARS layer-wise normalisation

name: Per-coordinate adaptive step sizes
positive_test: scales each coordinate's step by an accumulated statistic of its own gradients
negative_test: a single global step size for all coordinates
examples: AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adadelta, Adam, AdamW, AMSGrad, NAdam, RAdam, AdaBelief, Adafactor, LAMB, Sophia
notes: the single most frequent algorithm in the field

name: Matrix-preconditioned optimisation
characteristic: how the curvature matrix is approximated
positive_test: multiplies the gradient by an approximation of an inverse curvature matrix
negative_test: scaling coordinates independently
examples: L-BFGS, K-FAC, Shampoo, Muon

name: Quasi-Newton methods
positive_test: builds the inverse-Hessian approximation from successive gradient differences
negative_test: computing curvature from the model's Fisher or Gauss-Newton structure
examples: Newton's method, BFGS, L-BFGS, DFP, SR1

name: Natural-gradient and Kronecker preconditioners
positive_test: preconditions with the Fisher information or a Kronecker-factored surrogate of it
negative_test: secant-condition updates
examples: natural gradient, K-FAC, Shampoo, SOAP, Muon, PSGD

name: Matrix-free curvature methods
positive_test: solves the Newton system with Hessian-vector products instead of forming the matrix
negative_test: forming or factoring a curvature matrix explicitly
examples: conjugate gradient, Hessian-free optimisation, Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt

name: Trust-region control
positive_test: restricts each step to a region where the local model is trusted
negative_test: a fixed step size with no region constraint
examples: trust-region Newton, TRPO's KL region, Cauchy-point methods
notes: TRPO inherits from here and from policy gradients

name: Variance-reduced stochastic gradients
positive_test: corrects the stochastic gradient with a stored snapshot to shrink its variance
negative_test: plain minibatch sampling
examples: SAG, SVRG, SAGA, SARAH, SPIDER
notes: strong theory, thin practical uptake in deep learning

name: Proximal and splitting methods
characteristic: how the non-smooth part of the objective is handled
positive_test: handles a non-smooth term with a proximal operator or by splitting the problem
negative_test: taking a subgradient step on the non-smooth term
examples: proximal gradient, ISTA, FISTA, ADMM, coordinate descent, Frank-Wolfe, mirror descent
notes: the main vehicle for sparse classical estimators

name: Step-size and update schedules
characteristic: what the schedule is a function of
positive_test: changes the step size or other optimiser hyperparameter over the course of training
negative_test: changing the direction of the update
examples: cosine annealing, SGDR, one-cycle, warmup

name: Time-indexed schedules
positive_test: the step size is a fixed function of the iteration or epoch index
negative_test: a schedule reacting to observed loss
examples: step decay, exponential decay, polynomial decay, cosine annealing, SGDR, linear warmup, WSD

name: Feedback-driven schedules
positive_test: the step size changes in response to a measured training statistic
negative_test: a schedule computable in advance
examples: ReduceLROnPlateau, adaptive gradient clipping, loss-based restarts

name: Scaling-rule hyperparameter transfer
positive_test: sets step sizes by a width or compute scaling law transferred from a smaller model
negative_test: tuning the step size on the target model directly
examples: muP, muTransfer, linear batch-size scaling rule, square-root scaling

name: Gradient post-processing
characteristic: what the gradient is modified to satisfy
positive_test: modifies the gradient between backward pass and update step
negative_test: modifying the loss, or the update rule's state
examples: gradient clipping, gradient accumulation, PCGrad, DP-SGD clipping

name: Norm and value clipping
positive_test: rescales or truncates the gradient when it exceeds a threshold
negative_test: adding noise or projecting onto another gradient
examples: global-norm clipping, value clipping, adaptive gradient clipping, per-sample clipping

name: Multi-objective gradient surgery
positive_test: alters per-task gradients to remove mutual interference before summing
negative_test: weighting task losses as scalars
examples: PCGrad, CAGrad, GradDrop, GradNorm

name: Privacy-noised gradients
positive_test: clips per-example gradients and adds calibrated noise to meet a privacy budget
negative_test: clipping without a noise mechanism or accountant
examples: DP-SGD, DP-Adam, DP-FTRL

name: Weight averaging and merging
characteristic: over what the parameters are averaged
positive_test: produces a parameter vector by combining several parameter vectors
negative_test: combining predictions rather than parameters
examples: Polyak averaging, EMA, SWA

name: Averaging along one trajectory
positive_test: averages iterates produced by a single training run
negative_test: averaging independently trained models
examples: Polyak-Ruppert averaging, EMA of weights, SWA, LAWA, checkpoint averaging

name: Merging independently trained models
positive_test: combines parameters of separately finetuned models into one
negative_test: averaging checkpoints from one run
examples: model soups, task arithmetic, TIES-merging, DARE, SLERP merge, Fisher merging
notes: role is parameter rewriting, not fitting

name: Parameter initialisation schemes
characteristic: what statistic the initialisation is designed to preserve
positive_test: sets the initial parameter distribution by an explicit named rule
negative_test: a learned or pretrained initialisation
examples: LeCun init, Xavier/Glorot, He init, orthogonal init, LSUV, Fixup, muP init
notes: boundary with architecture; see Tensions

name: Expectation-maximisation
positive_test: alternates computing responsibilities under the current parameters and maximising the expected complete-data likelihood
negative_test: optimising the marginal likelihood by direct gradient ascent
examples: EM, generalised EM, variational EM, Baum-Welch, hard EM
notes: the classical-statistics counterpart of an optimiser

name: Derivative-free optimisation
characteristic: how new candidate points are proposed
positive_test: searches parameter or configuration space using only function evaluations
negative_test: using analytic or automatic gradients
examples: CMA-ES, genetic algorithms, Nelder-Mead, simulated annealing

name: Evolution strategies
positive_test: samples a population from a distribution and updates that distribution's parameters
negative_test: recombining discrete genotypes
examples: NES, CMA-ES, sep-CMA-ES, OpenAI-ES, Augmented Random Search

name: Genetic and evolutionary programming
positive_test: uses crossover and mutation over structured individuals with selection
negative_test: updating a parametric search distribution
examples: genetic algorithms, NEAT, regularised evolution, genetic programming

name: Direct local search
positive_test: moves a simplex or pattern of points by comparison of function values
negative_test: maintaining a population or a probabilistic model
examples: Nelder-Mead, pattern search, Powell's method, coordinate search

name: Annealed stochastic search
positive_test: accepts worsening moves with a temperature-controlled probability
negative_test: greedy acceptance only
examples: simulated annealing, parallel tempering, basin hopping

name: Closed-form and spectral estimators
characteristic: which matrix problem the estimate reduces to
positive_test: obtains parameters by solving an equation or decomposition, not by iterating a step rule
negative_test: any iterative descent procedure
examples: normal equations, QR least squares, ridge closed form, truncated SVD, method of moments
notes: the home for "no optimiser was used"

name: Explicit regularisation
characteristic: what the penalty or perturbation is applied to
positive_test: adds a term or perturbation whose purpose is to constrain the solution, not to fit the data
negative_test: a term that encodes the task target
examples: weight decay, dropout, label smoothing, SAM

name: Parameter-norm penalties
positive_test: penalises a norm or spectral property of the parameters
negative_test: perturbing activations or inputs
examples: L2/weight decay, decoupled weight decay, L1, max-norm, spectral norm, orthogonality penalties

name: Stochastic activation regularisation
positive_test: randomly removes or perturbs units or paths during training only
negative_test: a deterministic penalty term
examples: dropout, DropConnect, stochastic depth, DropBlock, DropPath, LayerDrop
notes: partly a layer, partly a procedure

name: Target smoothing
positive_test: softens or perturbs the training target rather than the model
negative_test: perturbing the input
examples: label smoothing, confidence penalty, mixup labels, temperature-softened targets

name: Consistency regularisation
positive_test: penalises disagreement between the model's outputs on two perturbed versions of one input
negative_test: penalising disagreement with an external label
examples: Pi-model, temporal ensembling, Mean Teacher, VAT, UDA, R-Drop

name: Loss-geometry regularisation
positive_test: explicitly seeks flat minima or bounds a derivative of the loss surface
negative_test: penalising parameter magnitude
examples: SAM, ASAM, GSAM, gradient penalty, Jacobian/Hessian penalties

name: Stopping and checkpoint selection
characteristic: what signal triggers the stop
positive_test: decides when training ends or which checkpoint is kept
negative_test: deciding how large a step to take
examples: early stopping, patience rules, best-checkpoint selection, validation-plateau stopping

name: Semi-supervised learning
characteristic: how an unlabelled example is given a target
positive_test: uses labelled and unlabelled data in one fitting procedure
negative_test: pretraining on unlabelled data then finetuning separately
examples: FixMatch, Noisy Student, label propagation

name: Self-training and pseudo-labelling
positive_test: labels unlabelled data with the current model and retrains on confident predictions
negative_test: deriving the target from a transformation rather than a prediction
examples: self-training, pseudo-labelling, Noisy Student, FixMatch, FlexMatch, SoftMatch
notes: FixMatch is multi-parent with consistency

name: Interpolation-based semi-supervision
positive_test: mixes labelled and unlabelled examples and their guessed labels
negative_test: training on each example separately
examples: MixMatch, ReMixMatch, ICT

name: Graph-based label propagation
positive_test: spreads labels across a similarity graph built over labelled and unlabelled points
negative_test: assigning labels by a parametric model's prediction
examples: label propagation, label spreading, harmonic functions

name: Weak supervision and label aggregation
positive_test: combines noisy labelling rules or annotators into probabilistic labels
negative_test: using a single trusted label source
examples: Snorkel/data programming, Dawid-Skene, MACE, majority-vote aggregation

name: Multi-view co-training
positive_test: two or more learners on different views label data for one another
negative_test: a single learner labelling its own data
examples: co-training, tri-training, democratic co-learning

name: Domain adaptation and invariance
characteristic: what quantity is aligned across domains
positive_test: trains with data from a source domain to perform on a shifted target domain
negative_test: adapting after deployment with no training-time target data
examples: DANN, CORAL, IRM

name: Adversarial domain alignment
positive_test: trains a domain discriminator the feature extractor is trained to fool
negative_test: matching moments or kernels in closed form
examples: DANN, ADDA, CDAN, MDD

name: Statistic-matching alignment
positive_test: minimises an explicit discrepancy between source and target feature statistics
negative_test: using a learned discriminator
examples: CORAL, Deep CORAL, MMD/DAN, JAN, optimal-transport alignment

name: Invariant risk and environment-based objectives
positive_test: requires the optimal predictor to be simultaneously optimal across labelled environments
negative_test: aligning marginal feature distributions
examples: IRM, REx, GroupDRO, Fish, CLOvE

name: Distributional and adversarial robustness
characteristic: what adversary the objective is minimised against
positive_test: minimises a worst-case rather than an average risk
negative_test: minimising the empirical mean loss
examples: DRO, PGD adversarial training, randomised smoothing

name: Distributionally robust optimisation
positive_test: minimises the worst-case loss over a set of reweightings of the training distribution
negative_test: minimising worst case over input perturbations
examples: DRO, CVaR-DRO, GroupDRO, chi-square DRO

name: Adversarial training
positive_test: solves an inner maximisation over input perturbations inside each training step
negative_test: perturbing inputs without maximising the loss
examples: PGD adversarial training, TRADES, MART, FastAT, free adversarial training

name: Certified robustness
positive_test: returns a provable guarantee of invariance within a stated input region
negative_test: providing only empirical attack resistance
examples: randomised smoothing, IBP, CROWN, convex relaxations

name: Multi-task and auxiliary objectives
characteristic: how multiple losses are combined
positive_test: fits one parameter set against two or more distinct task losses
negative_test: finetuning sequentially, one task at a time
examples: uniform weighting, uncertainty weighting, GradNorm, UNREAL auxiliary tasks

name: Meta-learning
characteristic: what quantity is meta-learned
positive_test: optimises across a distribution of tasks so that per-task adaptation is cheap
negative_test: training on one task distribution with no inner adaptation loop
examples: MAML, prototypical networks, RL-squared

name: Optimisation-based meta-learning
positive_test: meta-learns an initialisation whose few-step adaptation performs well
negative_test: meta-learning a metric or a black-box update
examples: MAML, FOMAML, Reptile, ANIL, Meta-SGD, iMAML

name: Metric-based few-shot learning
positive_test: classifies by distance to class representatives in a learned embedding
negative_test: updating parameters per task
examples: Siamese networks, Matching Networks, Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks

name: Black-box and in-context adaptation
positive_test: adaptation happens in activations or recurrent state, with no parameter update
negative_test: adapting by gradient steps at task time
examples: RL-squared, SNAIL, in-context learning as meta-learning
notes: partly speculative as a *training* procedure

name: Learned optimisers
positive_test: meta-trains a parametric update rule applied to another model's parameters
negative_test: using a hand-designed update rule
examples: learning to learn by gradient descent, VeLO, L2O
notes: the learned optimiser is a model; the meta-training is the algorithm

name: Continual learning
characteristic: how interference with earlier tasks is resisted
positive_test: trains on a sequence of tasks without full access to earlier data
negative_test: training on all tasks jointly
examples: EWC, A-GEM, iCaRL

name: Importance-weighted parameter anchoring
positive_test: penalises movement of parameters deemed important to earlier tasks
negative_test: storing and replaying earlier examples
examples: EWC, SI, MAS, Riemannian walk

name: Rehearsal
positive_test: stores or regenerates earlier examples and mixes them into current training
negative_test: constraining parameters without any stored data
examples: experience replay, GEM, A-GEM, DER, iCaRL, generative replay

name: Capacity isolation
positive_test: allocates disjoint parameters or masks per task
negative_test: sharing all parameters across tasks
examples: progressive networks, PackNet, HAT, supermasks

name: Gradient projection
positive_test: projects updates onto directions that do not disturb earlier-task outputs
negative_test: penalising parameter movement isotropically
examples: orthogonal gradient descent, GPM, Adam-NSCL

name: Parameter-efficient adaptation
characteristic: where the new degrees of freedom live
positive_test: adapts a pretrained model while updating only a small fraction of, or an addition to, its parameters
negative_test: updating every parameter of the pretrained model
examples: LoRA, adapters, prefix tuning, BitFit

name: Inserted adapter modules
positive_test: inserts new trainable submodules into the frozen network and trains only those
negative_test: reparameterising existing weight matrices
examples: Houlsby adapters, Pfeiffer adapters, AdapterFusion, Compacter, Parallel adapters

name: Low-rank weight reparameterisation
positive_test: adds a trainable low-rank update to existing weight matrices, mergeable at inference
negative_test: adding modules that change the computation graph at inference
examples: LoRA, QLoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, LoRA+, ReLoRA, VeRA

name: Prompt and prefix tuning
positive_test: trains continuous vectors prepended to the input or to the attention keys and values
negative_test: training weights inside the network
examples: prefix tuning, prompt tuning, P-tuning v2, soft prompts

name: Sparse parameter selection
positive_test: trains a chosen sparse subset of the existing parameters
negative_test: adding new parameters of any kind
examples: BitFit, IA3, diff pruning, Fish-Mask, surgical finetuning

name: Freezing and staged unfreezing
positive_test: holds some existing layers fixed and trains the rest, with no new parameters beyond a head
negative_test: training all layers from the first step
examples: linear probing, feature extraction, gradual unfreezing, ULMFiT schedule, LP-FT

name: Supervised adaptation recipes
characteristic: what the demonstration data is and how it is composed
positive_test: finetunes a pretrained model on labelled demonstrations of the target behaviour
negative_test: fitting from random initialisation
examples: BERT finetuning, FLAN, Alpaca-style SFT

name: Instruction tuning
positive_test: finetunes on instruction-response pairs across many tasks to induce instruction following
negative_test: finetuning on a single downstream task
examples: FLAN, T0, Natural Instructions, Alpaca, Tulu-style SFT

name: Single-task finetuning
positive_test: adapts a pretrained model to one labelled downstream task
negative_test: multi-task instruction mixtures
examples: BERT finetuning, ULMFiT, task-specific heads

name: Data-parallel training
characteristic: how and when workers exchange their updates
positive_test: replicates the model across workers that process different data and combine gradients
negative_test: splitting the model itself across devices
examples: synchronous all-reduce SGD, Hogwild!, local SGD

name: Synchronous gradient aggregation
positive_test: every worker's gradient is combined before any worker steps
negative_test: workers step on stale or partial information
examples: synchronous SGD, ring all-reduce, large-batch recipes with LARS/LAMB

name: Asynchronous and stale updates
positive_test: workers apply updates without waiting, tolerating staleness
negative_test: a global barrier per step
examples: Hogwild!, Downpour SGD, ASGD, stale-synchronous parallel

name: Infrequent communication
positive_test: workers take several local steps before any averaging
negative_test: averaging after every single step
examples: local SGD, post-local SGD, EASGD, DiLoCo, FedAvg-style local steps
notes: shares its idea with federated averaging

name: Communicated-update compression
positive_test: quantises, sparsifies or low-rank-projects the tensor that is communicated
negative_test: changing the communication schedule only
examples: 1-bit SGD, QSGD, Deep Gradient Compression, PowerSGD, top-k sparsification

name: Decentralised and gossip training
positive_test: workers exchange only with neighbours, with no global aggregation step
negative_test: a central server or a global all-reduce
examples: D-PSGD, SGP, gossip averaging, AD-PSGD

name: Model-state sharding and pipelining
characteristic: which dimension of the computation is split across devices
positive_test: splits one model's parameters, activations or layers across devices
negative_test: replicating the full model on every device
examples: ZeRO, FSDP, Megatron tensor parallel, GPipe

name: Optimiser-state and parameter sharding
positive_test: partitions optimiser state, gradients or parameters across data-parallel ranks
negative_test: partitioning the computation of a single layer
examples: ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, ZeRO-3, FSDP, ZeRO-Offload, ZeRO-Infinity

name: Intra-layer tensor parallelism
positive_test: splits a single matrix multiplication across devices
negative_test: assigning whole layers to devices
examples: Megatron-LM tensor parallelism, sequence parallelism, 2D/2.5D parallel

name: Pipeline parallelism
positive_test: assigns consecutive layer blocks to devices and streams microbatches through them
negative_test: splitting within a layer
examples: GPipe, PipeDream, 1F1B, interleaved pipeline, zero-bubble pipeline

name: Sparse-expert routing
positive_test: routes each token or example to a subset of experts and balances the load
negative_test: dense computation on all parameters
examples: top-k gating, Switch routing, expert-choice routing, BASE layers, load-balancing losses
notes: boundary with architecture; routing itself is a procedure

name: Context and sequence sharding
positive_test: splits one long sequence's attention computation across devices
negative_test: splitting the batch
examples: ring attention, context parallelism, Blockwise parallel transformers

name: Memory-compute trade-offs
characteristic: what is recomputed or moved rather than stored
positive_test: reduces memory by recomputing or relocating intermediate state
negative_test: reducing memory by changing the model
examples: gradient checkpointing, selective recompute, CPU offload, mixed-precision training, loss scaling
notes: boundary: closer to systems than to learning

name: Federated learning
characteristic: what is changed relative to the local-steps-then-average loop
positive_test: trains across clients that never transmit their raw data
negative_test: centralised training on pooled data
examples: FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD

name: Federated averaging and its corrections
positive_test: averages client models after local epochs, with corrections for client drift
negative_test: personalising a separate model per client
examples: FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedNova, FedOpt, FedAdam

name: Personalised federated learning
positive_test: each client keeps a model that differs from the global one by design
negative_test: producing a single shared global model
examples: Per-FedAvg, pFedMe, FedRep, Ditto, FedBN

name: Federated system procedures
positive_test: changes which clients participate, when, or how updates are buffered
negative_test: changes the aggregation rule's mathematics
examples: client selection, FedBuff, asynchronous FL, split learning, hierarchical FL

name: Privacy-preserving training
characteristic: what the privacy mechanism protects against
positive_test: provides a stated privacy property for the training data
negative_test: a method whose privacy claim is only informal
examples: DP-SGD, PATE, secure aggregation

name: Differentially private learning
positive_test: bounds any single example's influence and accounts for a cumulative epsilon
negative_test: protecting data in transit without an epsilon bound
examples: DP-SGD, DP-Adam, DP-FTRL, PATE, DP-FedAvg

name: Cryptographic aggregation
positive_test: hides individual updates from the aggregator using a cryptographic protocol
negative_test: adding statistical noise to the update
examples: secure aggregation, homomorphic-encryption aggregation, secure multiparty computation

name: Machine unlearning
positive_test: removes a specific training example's influence from an already-trained model
negative_test: preventing influence from being recorded in the first place
examples: SISA, influence-function unlearning, certified removal, exact retraining shards

name: Hyperparameter optimisation
characteristic: how the next configuration is chosen
positive_test: runs multiple training trials to select hyperparameters by a validation signal
negative_test: picking hyperparameters by hand or by citation
examples: grid search, TPE, Hyperband, PBT

name: Enumerative and random search
positive_test: draws configurations from a fixed design with no adaptation to past trials
negative_test: choosing the next point from previous results
examples: grid search, random search, Sobol/quasi-random, Latin hypercube
notes: random search is the baseline everyone must beat

name: Surrogate-model search
positive_test: fits a probabilistic surrogate to past trials and maximises an acquisition function
negative_test: allocating budget without modelling the response surface
examples: GP-EI Bayesian optimisation, TPE, SMAC, BOHB, BORE

name: Budget-allocation search
positive_test: reallocates compute across running trials by early-stopping the weak ones
negative_test: running every trial to completion
examples: successive halving, Hyperband, ASHA, BOHB, PBT

name: Gradient-based hyperparameter optimisation
positive_test: differentiates a validation loss with respect to hyperparameters
negative_test: treating the trial as a black box
examples: hypergradient descent, implicit differentiation, DARTS-style relaxation

name: Transferred and predicted configurations
positive_test: sets hyperparameters from a scaling rule or a meta-model, without search on the target
negative_test: searching directly at the target scale
examples: muTransfer, meta-learned priors, scaling-law extrapolation, zero-shot HPO

name: Neural architecture search
characteristic: how the architecture space is traversed
positive_test: searches over architectures using a measured or predicted performance signal
negative_test: designing the architecture by hand
examples: NASNet, DARTS, Once-for-All
notes: the product is a model; the search is the algorithm

name: Controller-based search
positive_test: trains a controller policy that emits architectures, rewarded by their accuracy
negative_test: mutating a population or relaxing the space
examples: NASNet/Zoph-Le, ENAS, MetaQNN

name: Evolutionary architecture search
positive_test: mutates and selects architectures in a population
negative_test: following a gradient through architecture weights
examples: AmoebaNet/regularised evolution, NEAT, hierarchical evolution

name: Differentiable architecture search
positive_test: relaxes discrete choices into continuous weights and follows their gradient
negative_test: evaluating discrete candidates separately
examples: DARTS, PC-DARTS, GDAS, ProxylessNAS, SNAS

name: Supernet and weight-sharing search
positive_test: trains one over-parameterised network whose subnetworks are the candidates
negative_test: training each candidate from scratch
examples: one-shot NAS, Once-for-All, BigNAS, SPOS

name: Training-free architecture scoring
positive_test: ranks architectures by a proxy computable without training
negative_test: ranking by measured post-training accuracy
examples: zero-cost proxies, NASWOT, synflow score

name: Pipeline and algorithm selection
characteristic: what part of the pipeline is searched
positive_test: searches jointly over preprocessing, model family and hyperparameters
negative_test: searching hyperparameters of a fixed model family
examples: Auto-WEKA, auto-sklearn, TPOT, AutoGluon, H2O AutoML

name: Pruning
characteristic: what score decides which parameters are removed
positive_test: sets a subset of parameters to zero and removes them from the computation
negative_test: lowering the numeric precision of all parameters
examples: magnitude pruning, lottery ticket, SparseGPT

name: Curvature-based saliency pruning
positive_test: scores parameters by an estimated loss increase from removing them
negative_test: scoring by magnitude alone
examples: OBD, OBS, WoodFisher, SNIP, GraSP

name: Magnitude and movement pruning
positive_test: removes the smallest weights, or those moving toward zero during finetuning
negative_test: estimating a second-order saliency
examples: magnitude pruning, iterative magnitude pruning, lottery ticket, movement pruning, RigL

name: Structured pruning
positive_test: removes whole channels, heads, layers or structured blocks
negative_test: removing individual scattered weights
examples: channel pruning, head pruning, LLM-Pruner, 2:4 structured sparsity, ShortGPT

name: One-shot post-training pruning
positive_test: prunes a trained model using a small calibration set and a local reconstruction
negative_test: pruning during training with retraining between steps
examples: SparseGPT, Wanda, Optimal BERT Surgeon

name: Quantization
characteristic: whether and how the network is retrained to the quantized grid
positive_test: reduces the numeric precision of weights or activations
negative_test: removing parameters entirely
examples: GPTQ, LSQ, BinaryConnect

name: Post-training quantization
positive_test: quantises a finished model using only a small calibration set, with no gradient training
negative_test: training the model with quantization in the loop
examples: min-max calibration, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, LLM.int8, QuIP, SpQR

name: Quantization-aware training
positive_test: simulates quantization in the forward pass and trains through a straight-through estimator
negative_test: calibrating without any training
examples: QAT, LSQ, PACT, DoReFa

name: Binarisation and ternarisation
positive_test: reduces weights or activations to one or two bits
negative_test: reducing to 4 or 8 bits
examples: BinaryConnect, XNOR-Net, BNN, TWN

name: Inference-cache quantization
positive_test: quantises the attention cache rather than the parameters
negative_test: quantising weights
examples: KV-cache quantization, KIVI, per-channel cache scaling

name: Knowledge distillation
characteristic: what of the teacher is matched
positive_test: trains a student against targets produced by a teacher model
negative_test: training against ground-truth labels only
examples: Hinton KD, FitNets, DistilBERT
notes: role is objective; compression is a goal, not a slot

name: Output-distribution distillation
positive_test: matches the teacher's softened output distribution
negative_test: matching internal representations
examples: Hinton KD, born-again networks, DistilBERT, decoupled KD, sequence-level KD

name: Representation distillation
positive_test: matches internal activations, attention maps or relations
negative_test: matching outputs only
examples: FitNets, attention transfer, CRD, relational KD, TinyBERT

name: Self-distillation
positive_test: teacher and student are the same architecture, or the model's own earlier state
negative_test: a strictly larger separate teacher
examples: born-again networks, self-distillation, BAN, deep mutual learning

name: Weight factorisation
characteristic: which decomposition is applied
positive_test: replaces a weight tensor with a product of smaller factors
negative_test: zeroing or requantising the original tensor
examples: SVD compression, Tucker decomposition, CP decomposition, ASVD
notes: speculative: often reported without a name

name: Sequence decoding
characteristic: how the next output is chosen from the model's scores
positive_test: converts the model's scores into an emitted sequence at inference time
negative_test: changing what the model scores
examples: beam search, nucleus sampling, speculative decoding
notes: decides what is selected, so it decides what the model says

name: Greedy decoding
positive_test: emits the argmax at every step with no lookahead and no sampling
negative_test: keeping multiple hypotheses or sampling
examples: greedy decoding, argmax decoding

name: Beam search
positive_test: maintains a fixed number of partial hypotheses ranked by cumulative score
negative_test: keeping only one hypothesis, or sampling
examples: beam search, length-normalised beam, diverse beam search, constrained beam search

name: Truncated stochastic sampling
positive_test: samples from the output distribution after reshaping or truncating its tail
negative_test: deterministic selection
examples: ancestral sampling, temperature, top-k, nucleus/top-p, typical sampling, min-p, eta sampling, Mirostat

name: Contrastive decoding
positive_test: scores a token by the difference between two models' or two layers' log-probabilities
negative_test: scoring with a single distribution
examples: contrastive decoding, DoLa, context-aware decoding, contrastive search

name: Constrained decoding
positive_test: masks tokens that would violate a grammar, schema or lexical constraint
negative_test: rejecting invalid outputs after generation
examples: grammar-constrained decoding, FSM-constrained decoding, lexically constrained decoding, JSON-schema decoding

name: Candidate reranking and MBR
positive_test: generates a candidate set and selects among complete candidates by a utility
negative_test: selecting token by token
examples: MBR decoding, reranking by model score, n-best reranking, quality-estimation reranking

name: Speculative decoding
positive_test: a cheap proposer drafts tokens that the target model verifies in parallel
negative_test: a single model emitting one token per forward pass
examples: speculative decoding, Medusa, EAGLE, lookahead decoding, self-speculative decoding
notes: changes cost, not the output distribution

name: Guided generation
positive_test: perturbs the output distribution with an auxiliary scorer or an unconditional contrast
negative_test: selecting from the unmodified distribution
examples: classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance, PPLM, FUDGE, GeDi
notes: shared with the diffusion lineage

name: Test-time search and deliberation
characteristic: what structure the search explores
positive_test: spends extra inference compute exploring multiple reasoning or action paths
negative_test: a single forward pass per output
examples: self-consistency, tree of thoughts, MCTS

name: Sample-and-select
positive_test: samples several complete attempts and selects or aggregates among them
negative_test: expanding a partial solution
examples: best-of-n, self-consistency majority vote, weighted best-of-n, rejection sampling at inference

name: Structured reasoning search
positive_test: expands and scores partial reasoning states in a tree or graph
negative_test: generating one linear chain
examples: chain-of-thought prompting, least-to-most, tree of thoughts, graph of thoughts, PRM-guided beam, MCTS-guided decoding
notes: CoT is a named procedure, so it is admissible

name: Iterative refinement loops
positive_test: re-invokes the model on its own previous output plus feedback, in a loop
negative_test: a single generation with no revision
examples: ReAct, Reflexion, self-refine, self-debug, multi-agent debate

name: Explicit planning over a model
positive_test: searches over an environment or dynamics model to choose an action
negative_test: choosing an action by a direct policy forward pass
examples: A-star, Dijkstra, MCTS, UCT, PUCT, CEM-MPC, MPPI, iLQR, DDP
notes: shared with model-based RL

name: Retrieval and context construction
characteristic: how candidate context is scored
positive_test: selects external items to place in the model's input at inference
negative_test: selecting training examples before fitting
examples: BM25, DPR, RAG

name: Lexical retrieval
positive_test: scores documents by weighted term overlap with the query
negative_test: scoring by learned dense vectors
examples: TF-IDF, BM25, BM25+, SPLADE (hybrid)

name: Learned dense retrieval
positive_test: scores by inner product of learned query and document embeddings
negative_test: scoring by term statistics
examples: DSSM, DPR, ANCE, ColBERT, E5, GTE
notes: trained contrastively, used at inference

name: Approximate nearest-neighbour search
positive_test: finds approximate nearest neighbours under an index structure with a recall-speed trade-off
negative_test: exhaustive exact search
examples: LSH, IVF-PQ, HNSW, DiskANN, ScaNN

name: Retrieval-augmented generation
positive_test: conditions generation on retrieved passages, possibly trained jointly
negative_test: retrieving without feeding the result to a generator
examples: kNN-LM, REALM, RAG, FiD, RETRO, Self-RAG

name: Retrieval reranking and fusion
positive_test: re-scores or merges candidate lists from a first-stage retriever
negative_test: producing the first-stage candidates
examples: cross-encoder reranking, monoT5, reciprocal rank fusion, ColBERT late interaction

name: Calibration and uncertainty quantification
characteristic: what produces the uncertainty estimate
positive_test: converts model outputs into calibrated probabilities, intervals or abstentions
negative_test: changing which output is emitted
examples: temperature scaling, conformal prediction, deep ensembles

name: Post-hoc probability recalibration
positive_test: fits a small mapping from scores to probabilities on a held-out split
negative_test: producing uncertainty from multiple models or a posterior
examples: Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling, vector and matrix scaling, beta calibration

name: Conformal prediction
positive_test: produces sets or intervals with a finite-sample coverage guarantee under exchangeability
negative_test: producing a point probability with no coverage guarantee
examples: split conformal, full conformal, CQR, conformal risk control, adaptive conformal

name: Ensemble-based uncertainty
positive_test: estimates uncertainty from disagreement across independently trained or sampled models
negative_test: estimating from one model's output distribution
examples: deep ensembles, snapshot ensembles, batch ensembles, hyper-ensembles

name: Approximate Bayesian neural inference
positive_test: approximates a posterior over parameters and marginalises predictions over it
negative_test: fitting a single point estimate
examples: Laplace approximation, Bayes-by-backprop, MC dropout, SWAG, SGLD posteriors

name: Out-of-distribution and selective prediction
positive_test: scores whether an input is outside the training distribution and may abstain
negative_test: calibrating probabilities on in-distribution data
examples: max-softmax baseline, ODIN, Mahalanobis score, energy-based OOD, selective prediction

name: Test-time adaptation
characteristic: what is updated at test time
positive_test: updates the model or its statistics using unlabelled test data during deployment
negative_test: adapting with labelled target data before deployment
examples: TENT, TTT, SHOT
notes: adapting at test time is a property of the method, not its use

name: Normalisation-statistic adaptation
positive_test: recomputes normalisation statistics on test batches, updating no weights
negative_test: updating weights by an optimisation step
examples: BN-statistic adaptation, DUA, prediction-time BN

name: Entropy-minimisation adaptation
positive_test: takes gradient steps on the entropy or a confidence surrogate of test predictions
negative_test: taking steps on a self-supervised auxiliary loss
examples: TENT, EATA, SAR, CoTTA, RoTTA

name: Self-supervised test-time training
positive_test: takes gradient steps on an auxiliary self-supervised loss computed on the test input
negative_test: using the task head's own entropy
examples: TTT, TTT-MAE, MEMO, TTT-layers

name: Prototype and classifier-only adaptation
positive_test: re-estimates class prototypes or the classifier head from test features
negative_test: updating the feature extractor
examples: SHOT, T3A, prototype refinement

name: Inference-time aggregation
characteristic: over what the predictions are combined
positive_test: combines several models' or several runs' predictions into one output
negative_test: combining their parameters instead
examples: voting, averaging, stacking, Bayesian model averaging, mixture-of-experts routing at inference

name: Attribution and interpretation
characteristic: what the explanation is computed from
positive_test: produces an explanation of a trained model's behaviour as an output
negative_test: changing the model's predictions
examples: Grad-CAM, SHAP, activation patching
notes: an explanation is an output, so the participant rule admits this

name: Gradient-based attribution
positive_test: attributes using gradients or gradient paths through the network
negative_test: attributing by perturbing inputs and refitting a surrogate
examples: saliency maps, Grad-CAM, integrated gradients, SmoothGrad, GradientSHAP

name: Perturbation-based attribution
positive_test: attributes by measuring output change under input occlusion or resampling
negative_test: reading internal gradients
examples: LIME, SHAP, occlusion, permutation importance, ablation studies

name: Probing and representation analysis
positive_test: fits or compares a simple readout on frozen internal representations
negative_test: explaining a single prediction
examples: linear probing, CKA, SVCCA, causal tracing, activation patching

name: Feature dictionary learning
positive_test: fits an overcomplete sparse basis over activations to name internal features
negative_test: attributing to input dimensions
examples: sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning on activations, transcoders

name: Fairness-constrained procedures
characteristic: at which stage the fairness constraint is applied
positive_test: enforces a stated group or individual fairness criterion as part of the procedure
negative_test: measuring disparity without acting on it
examples: reweighing, adversarial debiasing, equalized-odds post-processing

name: Pre-processing fairness interventions
positive_test: modifies the data before fitting so that a disparity criterion is reduced
negative_test: modifying the loss or the predictions
examples: reweighing, disparate impact remover, fair representation learning, LFR

name: In-processing fairness constraints
positive_test: adds a fairness constraint or penalty to the training objective
negative_test: adjusting the trained model's thresholds
examples: constrained ERM, reductions approach, adversarial debiasing, fair regularisers

name: Post-processing fairness adjustment
positive_test: adjusts thresholds or outputs per group on a trained model
negative_test: retraining with a modified objective
examples: equalized-odds post-processing, reject-option classification, group-wise thresholds

name: Linear and generalized linear estimation
characteristic: what penalty or link is added to least squares
positive_test: fits a linear predictor, possibly through a link function, to observed responses
negative_test: fitting a nonlinear function class
examples: OLS, ridge, lasso, logistic regression, GLM

name: Least-squares estimation
positive_test: minimises squared residuals with no penalty term
negative_test: adding a shrinkage penalty
examples: OLS, weighted least squares, generalised least squares, total least squares

name: Penalised regression
positive_test: adds a norm penalty on coefficients to the least-squares objective
negative_test: changing the loss on the residuals
examples: ridge, lasso, elastic net, group lasso, LARS, adaptive lasso, SCAD
notes: lasso doubles as feature selection

name: Generalized linear models
positive_test: maps a linear predictor through a link to a non-Gaussian response distribution
negative_test: using an identity link with Gaussian noise
examples: logistic regression, Poisson regression, negative binomial, ordinal and multinomial logit

name: Robust and quantile regression
positive_test: replaces squared loss with a loss bounded in the residual, or targets a quantile
negative_test: minimising mean squared error
examples: Huber regression, RANSAC, Theil-Sen, quantile regression, M-estimators

name: Hierarchical and mixed-effects models
positive_test: adds group-level random effects or a correlation structure to the linear predictor
negative_test: treating all observations as independent with one coefficient vector
examples: linear mixed models, GEE, multilevel models, random-effects meta-analysis

name: Kernel methods
characteristic: which learning problem the kernel is substituted into
positive_test: replaces inner products with a kernel so a linear method acts in a feature space
negative_test: computing explicit high-dimensional features and fitting linearly
examples: SVM, kernel ridge, kernel PCA

name: Margin-maximising classifiers
positive_test: maximises the margin to the separating surface, with slack for errors
negative_test: minimising a likelihood or squared error
examples: perceptron, hard and soft-margin SVM, SVR, one-class SVM, structured SVM

name: Kernelised least squares and components
positive_test: substitutes a kernel into a closed-form least-squares or eigen problem
negative_test: solving a hinge-loss quadratic program
examples: kernel ridge regression, kernel PCA, kernel k-means, kernel CCA

name: Kernel approximation
positive_test: approximates the kernel matrix with explicit random or sampled features
negative_test: computing the exact kernel matrix
examples: random Fourier features, Nystrom approximation, random kitchen sinks

name: Gaussian-process inference
characteristic: how the posterior is made tractable
positive_test: places a GP prior over functions and computes a posterior predictive distribution
negative_test: fitting point-estimate parameters with no function-space posterior
examples: GP regression, SVGP, deep GP

name: Exact GP regression
positive_test: inverts the full kernel matrix to obtain the exact posterior
negative_test: approximating with inducing points or a variational bound
examples: GP regression, GP with marginal-likelihood hyperparameter fitting

name: Sparse and approximate GPs
positive_test: summarises the data with inducing points or a variational posterior
negative_test: exact cubic-cost inference
examples: FITC, SVGP, SKI/KISS-GP, deep GP, GP classification by Laplace or EP

name: Decision-tree induction
characteristic: split criterion and pruning rule
positive_test: grows a tree by recursively partitioning the feature space on single-variable tests
negative_test: combining many trees as one predictor
examples: ID3, C4.5, CART, CHAID, conditional inference trees

name: Bootstrap aggregation
positive_test: averages predictors each fitted to a resampled version of the data
negative_test: fitting predictors sequentially on reweighted data
examples: bagging, random forest, extremely randomised trees, rotation forest

name: Boosting
positive_test: fits predictors sequentially, each targeting the previous ensemble's errors
negative_test: fitting predictors independently in parallel
examples: AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, NGBoost, LambdaMART
notes: the strongest tabular baseline family

name: Instance-based learning
positive_test: makes predictions directly from stored training examples with no fitted global model
negative_test: fitting parameters that summarise the data
examples: k-NN, weighted k-NN, condensed NN, Parzen windows/KDE, LOESS, RBF interpolation
notes: the canonical algorithm with no model

name: Generative classifiers
characteristic: what is assumed about the class-conditional density
positive_test: models each class's feature distribution and classifies by Bayes rule
negative_test: modelling the conditional label distribution directly
examples: naive Bayes, Gaussian/multinomial/Bernoulli NB, LDA, QDA, Bayesian network classifiers

name: Clustering
characteristic: what defines cluster membership
